romania.title: CNAIR: Au fost remediate problemele la plățile pe platforma TollRo. Sistemul poate prelua acum mai mult trafic. Anunțul lui Miruță
romania.summary: Platforma TollRo a întâmpinat mai multe disfuncționalități după lansarea Sistemului de Tarifare Electronică Rutieră, la 1 octombrie. CNAIR anunță că problemele legate de plata cu cardul și de capacitatea platformei au fost remediate, iar fluxul e-mailurilor de confirmare a conturilor a fost îmbunătățit. În primele 12 ore, platforma a avut aproximativ 4 milioane de accesări, au fost înregistrați 50.000 de utilizatori și 170.000 de vehicule și au fost efectuate peste 60.000 de plăți. Stabilizarea completă a sistemului este estimată în cel mult 72 de ore.

medical.title: Alzheimer's disease and aging reshape brain communication in different ways
medical.summary: Both normal aging and Alzheimer's change how different brain regions communicate with each other. But a new study from Lund University reveals that these alterations follow distinct patterns, with disease-related shifts distinguishable from those linked to normal aging. And the alterations seen in Alzheimer's patients appear early, even before cognitive symptoms emerge. The findings are published in Nature Neuroscience.

medical.title: PET scans reveal alpha cancer therapy isotope with new algorithm in first human test
medical.summary: A research team led by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (Berkeley Lab) has developed a new imaging technique that could allow modern medical scanners to image targeted alpha therapy (TAT), an emerging cancer therapy for the diagnosis and treatment of cancer. The advance could enable the widespread adoption of this new cancer therapy.

medical.title: Brain circuit remembers stresses to help shape reactions to them
medical.summary: Researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai have identified a previously overlooked brain circuit that helps explain how prior adversity can make the brain more reactive to future stress.

medical.title: New dressing design aims to fight wound infections while supporting skin repair
medical.summary: Roughly 1 million people in Germany are receiving treatment for chronic wounds caused by conditions ranging from circulatory disorders and pressure ulcers to diabetes-related foot problems. Treatment costs total some 7.5 billion euros annually, and patients endure considerable suffering.

medical.title: Endurance exercise rewires liver metabolism differently based on sex, study suggests
medical.summary: Exercise benefits nearly every part of the body, including the liver and metabolism. But new research from the University of Missouri School of Medicine suggests those benefits may not look the same in males and females. The findings are published in the journal Cell Reports.

medical.title: How the brain learns to predict what to fear based on past experiences
medical.summary: Rutgers researchers are revealing how the brain decides which sensory experiences previously associated with an adverse experience should trigger a fear response.

medical.title: How loss of the critical tumor suppressor p53 enables mutant cells to expand through normal tissue
medical.summary: A protein known as p53 is, of all tumor suppressors in human cancer, the most frequently altered by gene mutations. When mutations cause it to be absent or nonfunctional, its loss can allow populations of mutant cells to expand through normal tissue. Researchers have long known that loss of p53 does more than remove a block to cell growth. But how p53 loss changes tissue behavior to permit this growth remains unclear.

medical.title: A molecular switch syncs fat burning to the body clock, our diet and the temperature around us
medical.summary: Brown fat burns fuel to make heat, and this activity is controlled by the body clock: It drops during sleep and rises before waking. But a cold morning or a skipped meal makes demands the clock never planned for. How the body keeps to a fixed energy timetable while still improvising has long been a puzzle.

medical.title: Higher daily step counts linked to fewer mental health problems in early adolescence
medical.summary: Every extra walk to school, casual soccer game in the park or trip to the store could be doing more for teenage mental health than first thought, according to new research tracking thousands of adolescents in the U.S.

medical.title: Before the first bite: A missing gut protein may set the stage for peanut allergy
medical.summary: For most people, a peanut butter sandwich poses no threat. But for the roughly 1.6 million children in the United States with peanut allergy, exposure can trigger a life-threatening reaction. Why some individuals are susceptible while others are not has remained one of the most pressing unsolved questions in allergy research. A new study from the UNC School of Medicine points to an unexpected answer: The gut lining itself may be primed for allergy before a child ever encounters a peanut.

medical.title: Discovery explains how immune cells target DNA mutations to improve antibodies
medical.summary: Scientists at the Montreal Clinical Research Institute (IRCM), led by Université de Montréal medical professor Javier Di Noia, have shed light on a fundamental mystery in immunology: How do immune cells manage to concentrate a powerful mutagenic enzyme at precisely defined regions of DNA while largely sparing the rest of the genome from potentially dangerous damage?

medical.title: Sleep hours miss part of story: Young adults lose sleep quality, not hours, amid heat, noise and light
medical.summary: Between college dormitories and cramped apartments, young adults often live in environments that can be loud, bright or uncomfortable, making it difficult to reliably get a good night's sleep, according to Adwoa Dadzie, a doctoral candidate in biobehavioral health at Penn State.

medical.title: New recommendations for serrated polyposis syndrome
medical.summary: New consensus recommendations by the U.S. Multi-Society Task Force (MSTF) on Colorectal Cancer (CRC) address serrated polyposis syndrome (SPS), which is the most common gastrointestinal polyp syndrome yet is widely underrecognized and often goes undiagnosed. SPS is a clinical syndrome characterized by an increased number of serrated lesions and is associated with an increased risk of CRC.

medical.title: Novel treatment combination improves progression-free survival in most common form of metastatic breast cancer
medical.summary: Patients with estrogen receptor-positive (ER+), HER-2-negative advanced breast cancer experienced significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) when treated with an oral combination regimen that included giredestrant, a novel, next-generation selective ER degrader and full antagonist (SERD), compared with a standard combination approach. These findings, from the phase 3 evERA Breast Cancer study, were published today in the New England Journal of Medicine. Initial results of the evERA study were presented at the 2025 Congress of the European Society of Medical Oncology.

medical.title: Magnetic therapy headset shows improved cognitive function and mood in people with long COVID
medical.summary: A new study led by researchers from the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai and published in Brain Communications found that a transcranial low-amplitude magnetic field intervention delivered twice weekly into the brain through a noninvasive headset was associated with improvements in several measures of cognitive function and emotional well-being in people experiencing cognitive impairment associated with long COVID.

medical.title: Study finds hidden mutation rates may shape cancer risk
medical.summary: A new study by scientists at City of Hope and TGen, part of City of Hope, found surprisingly large differences in the number of mutations present in the organs of healthy individuals. Some study participants had mutation counts similar to those typically found in cancer patients. These results provide an explanation for why some individuals ultimately develop cancer, opening the door to improved approaches to cancer risk assessment and prevention.

medical.title: Initiative standardizes evaluation of ICU discharge readiness
medical.summary: A standardized process to evaluate patients for their readiness to be discharged from an intensive care unit (ICU) can help reduce readmissions while providing clarity and supporting collaboration among the interprofessional team, according to a study published in Critical Care Nurse.

medical.title: A major risk of breast cancer screening may have been overestimated for decades
medical.summary: A new analysis suggests mammograms may lead to far less breast cancer overdiagnosis than some earlier studies indicated. Researchers reexamined all eight major randomized screening trials and accounted for differences in follow-up time, screening frequency, and screening after trials ended. Their results were consistent with an overdiagnosis rate below 5%, rather than estimates approaching 30% to 50%.

medical.title: That fresh cleaning smell could be filling your home with nanoparticles
medical.summary: Researchers found that scented cleaners can react with ozone indoors to create billions or trillions of invisible nanoparticles that can penetrate deep into the lungs. The pollution forms within minutes and, in some cases, may produce an inhaled particle dose comparable to or greater than standing near heavy traffic.

medical.title: Zepbound and Mounjaro may turn on the body’s calorie-burning brown fat
medical.summary: Tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound, activated calorie-burning brown fat in obese mice, revealing a potential metabolic effect beyond appetite suppression. If confirmed in humans, the finding could help explain the drug’s powerful benefits and inspire more comprehensive treatments for obesity and diabetes.

medical.title: REM sleep paradox: Dreaming may drain the brain’s energy even as fuel supply rises
medical.summary: Scientists discovered a surprising energy paradox in the brain during REM sleep, the stage most closely associated with dreaming. Blood supply to the brain begins increasing even before REM starts, but neurons’ immediately available energy, measured as ATP, then drops. The finding suggests that dreaming may require such intense internal processing that neurons consume energy faster than it can be replenished.

medical.title: Don’t toss cannabis leaves: They may contain rare compounds with medical potential
medical.summary: Scientists discovered rare flavoalkaloids in Cannabis leaves for the first time, along with dozens of other phenolic compounds that had never been reported in the plant. The findings suggest that Cannabis leaves, often discarded as waste, may contain a surprisingly rich source of potentially useful chemicals.

medical.title: Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once
medical.summary: A new needle-thin brain implant can record neural activity, deliver drugs, and stimulate multiple brain regions using a single flexible fiber. Successful tests in mice suggest it could give scientists a more precise, less invasive way to study the brain and may eventually help treat neurological disorders such as epilepsy.

medical.title: Stanford scientists discover the human brain may actually be two separate organs
medical.summary: Scientists have found that the human brain develops from two distinct cellular systems, suggesting that evolution fused together two ancient nervous systems with very different jobs. The discovery also allowed researchers to grow human hindbrain neurons in the lab, opening new possibilities for studying ALS, spinal muscular atrophy, and other brainstem diseases.

science.title: RAB1 proteins help recruit membrane-building vesicles to mitochondria during mitochondria-selective autophagy
science.summary: The Intracellular Quality Control Project at the Tokyo Metropolitan Institute of Medical Science has identified a molecular mechanism that helps initiate the formation of autophagic membranes around damaged mitochondria.

science.title: How African restoration projects spill over into surrounding landscapes
science.summary: Researchers from the University of Sheffield and University of Cambridge have conducted the most comprehensive study to date on how habitat restoration in sub-Saharan Africa impacts tree loss beyond project boundaries.

science.title: Crystals thinner than human hair can move or partly dissolve when exposed to chloroform
science.summary: Many of the common materials we encounter in our daily lives are crystalline, including ice, salt and sugar. The crystal structures of some solids are formed from molecules arranged in simple geometric patterns, and these patterns can be changed to give the solids special properties required for high-tech applications. However, changing these connections requires extreme measures, such as high heat, leaving researchers with the challenge of finding an easier transformation method.

science.title: Pickpockets and poets—creating elite mindsets in soccer
science.summary: New research from NTNU's Department of Psychology indicates that elite soccer players experience lower levels of competitive anxiety than amateur players, despite performing under intense scrutiny.

science.title: Hidden 'funnels' let complex systems slip between stable states
science.summary: Many systems in nature can settle into several different stable states, with the final state depending on their starting conditions. However, the boundaries separating these states are often far more complicated than they first appear.

science.title: Trehalose analog provides a new platform for designing water-soluble glycopolymers
science.summary: Sugars are attractive building blocks for functional materials because of their high water affinity and diverse biological properties. Incorporating sugars into synthetic polymers can therefore provide materials that combine the processability of polymers with characteristics derived from carbohydrates. science.title: Desert alga reveals how fast growth and resistance to extreme conditions can coexist
science.summary: A single-celled green alga from the sand dunes of the Negev Desert has, within just a few years, become a key model organism in modern photosynthesis research. Chlorella ohadii helps researchers better understand plants' adaptability to extreme environmental conditions. These findings could help make crops more resilient to heat, drought, and other consequences of climate change in the future. Haim Treves, a professor of plant metabolism at RPTU, has been studying the desert alga since its discovery. His findings have now been published in the journal New Phytologist.

environment.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
environment.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

environment.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time

Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

mix_items.title: Crystals thinner than human hair can move or partly dissolve when exposed to chloroform
mix_items.summary: Many of the common materials we encounter in our daily lives are crystalline, including ice, salt and sugar. The crystal structures of some solids are formed from molecules arranged in simple geometric patterns, and these patterns can be changed to give the solids special properties required for high-tech applications. However, changing these connections requires extreme measures, such as high heat, leaving researchers with the challenge of finding an easier transformation method.

mix_items.summary: Researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai have identified a previously overlooked brain circuit that helps explain how prior adversity can make the brain more reactive to future stress.

mix_items.title: Pickpockets and poets—creating elite mindsets in soccer
mix_items.summary: New research from NTNU's Department of Psychology indicates that elite soccer players experience lower levels of competitive anxiety than amateur players, despite performing under intense scrutiny.

mix_items.title: Hidden 'funnels' let complex systems slip between stable states
mix_items.summary: Many systems in nature can settle into several different stable states, with the final state depending on their starting conditions. However, the boundaries separating these states are often far more complicated than they first appear.

mix_items.title: New dressing design aims to fight wound infections while supporting skin repair
mix_items.summary: Roughly 1 million people in Germany are receiving treatment for chronic wounds caused by conditions ranging from circulatory disorders and pressure ulcers to diabetes-related foot problems. Treatment costs total some 7.5 billion euros annually, and patients endure considerable suffering.

mix_items.title: Trehalose analog provides a new platform for designing water-soluble glycopolymers
mix_items.summary: Sugars are attractive building blocks for functional materials because of their high water affinity and diverse biological properties. Incorporating sugars into synthetic polymers can therefore provide materials that combine the processability of polymers with characteristics derived from carbohydrates. However, selective chemical modification of sugars is often challenging because they contain multiple hydroxyl groups with similar reactivities, making it difficult to introduce a polymerizable group at one defined position without multistep synthetic procedures.

mix_items.title: Python removal index identifies large females as key targets for limiting population growth
mix_items.summary: When it comes to removing Burmese pythons, one snake does not equal another. A new study by researchers at the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS) offers agencies a tool to identify pythons with the greatest influence on future population growth and uses machine learning to determine when they are most likely to be detected.

mix_items.title: Ultra-precise coatings help power the next generation of gravitational wave detectors
mix_items.summary: Researchers from The Australian National University (ANU) have engineered new optical coatings for LIGO, the global collaboration hunting gravitational waves from colliding black holes and neutron stars.

mix_items.title: Endurance exercise rewires liver metabolism differently based on sex, study suggests
mix_items.summary: Exercise benefits nearly every part of the body, including the liver and metabolism. But new research from the University of Missouri School of Medicine suggests those benefits may not look the same in males and females. The findings are published in the journal Cell Reports.

mix_items.title: How North Korean defectors help us understand refugee entrepreneurs
mix_items.summary: Refugees are more likely than native citizens to begin entrepreneurial ventures in their adopted countries, either by choice or because they have few other options. A new study offers insight into how refugees from common backgrounds end up adopting very different approaches to running their businesses by focusing on refugees who defected from North Korea and started their own ventures in South Korea.

mix_items.title: Desert alga reveals how fast growth and resistance to extreme conditions can coexist
mix_items.summary: A single-celled green alga from the sand dunes of the Negev Desert has, within just a few years, become a key model organism in modern photosynthesis research. Chlorella ohadii helps researchers better understand plants' adaptability to extreme environmental conditions. These findings could help make crops more resilient to heat, drought, and other consequences of climate change in the future. Haim Treves, a professor of plant metabolism at RPTU, has been studying the desert alga since its discovery. His findings have now been published in the journal New Phytologist.

mix_items.title: How the brain learns to predict what to fear based on past experiences
mix_items.summary: Rutgers researchers are revealing how the brain decides which sensory experiences previously associated with an adverse experience should trigger a fear response.

mix_items.summary: In this Oct. 1, 2026, photo, a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft launch from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. mix_items.title: True identity emerges from lived experience, not hidden essence, research finds
mix_items.summary: So, you're a people pleaser? A social chameleon? Perhaps you're an introvert or an extrovert.

mix_items.title: How loss of the critical tumor suppressor p53 enables mutant cells to expand through normal tissue
mix_items.summary: A protein known as p53 is, of all tumor suppressors in human cancer, the most frequently altered by gene mutations. When mutations cause it to be absent or nonfunctional, its loss can allow populations of mutant cells to expand through normal tissue. Researchers have long known that loss of p53 does more than remove a block to cell growth. But how p53 loss changes tissue behavior to permit this growth remains unclear.

mix_items.title: Precisely patterned molecular threads boost neuron growth and synapse formation in cell cultures
mix_items.summary: Northwestern University scientists have developed remarkably long, precisely patterned molecular threads that could open new possibilities for designing advanced materials. The scientists also discovered that these threads—called supramolecular polymers—can dramatically enhance brain cell activity. The study is published in the journal Science.

mix_items.title: A molecular switch syncs fat burning to the body clock, our diet and the temperature around us
mix_items.summary: Brown fat burns fuel to make heat, and this activity is controlled by the body clock: It drops during sleep and rises before waking. But a cold morning or a skipped meal makes demands the clock never planned for. How the body keeps to a fixed energy timetable while still improvising has long been a puzzle.

mix_items.title: Higher daily step counts linked to fewer mental health problems in early adolescence
mix_items.summary: Every extra walk to school, casual soccer game in the park or trip to the store could be doing more for teenage mental health than first thought, according to new research tracking thousands of adolescents in the U.S.

mix_items.title: Growth in milk boosts Staph bacteria's resistance to antibiotics, experiments reveal
mix_items.summary: Staphylococcus aureus is frequently found in human and veterinary infections. It is named for the golden-yellow pigment it produces, which contributes to its virulence and protects it against oxidative stress. Its ability to withstand antibiotic treatment makes it a major clinical challenge.

mix_items.title: Sea change: WildFin aims to improve fish behavior analysis in the wild
mix_items.summary: In the first year of her doctoral research, Abigail Grassick collected hours of underwater video as she studied fish communities living on bommies—individual clumps of coral—on the seafloor off the coast of Curaçao.

mix_items.title: Fluent in two languages? It comes at a cost to emotional regulation (but don't worry)
mix_items.summary: Say "I'm angry" out loud, and your brain reacts to it, reducing the use of emotional brain regions. But this trick does not work if you say it in your second language. A new study published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences shows that it doesn't work in any language if you are a balanced bilingual.

mix_items.title: Before the first bite: A missing gut protein may set the stage for peanut allergy
mix_items.summary: For most people, a peanut butter sandwich poses no threat. But for the roughly 1.6 million children in the United States with peanut allergy, exposure can trigger a life-threatening reaction. Why some individuals are susceptible while others are not has remained one of the most pressing unsolved questions in allergy research. A new study from the UNC School of Medicine points to an unexpected answer: The gut lining itself may be primed for allergy before a child ever encounters a peanut.

mix_items.title: Discovery explains how immune cells target DNA mutations to improve antibodies
mix_items.summary: Scientists at the Montreal Clinical Research Institute (IRCM), led by Université de Montréal medical professor Javier Di Noia, have shed light on a fundamental mystery in immunology: How do immune cells manage to concentrate a powerful mutagenic enzyme at precisely defined regions of DNA while largely sparing the rest of the genome from potentially dangerous damage?

mix_items.title: From suicide bombers to positions of authority—the changing role of women in jihadi groups
mix_items.summary: Khadra Essa, a Somali-born Dutch citizen operating in Syria under the name Umm Qaqa al-Somali, is a wanted woman.

mix_items.title: Sleep hours miss part of story: Young adults lose sleep quality, not hours, amid heat, noise and light
mix_items.summary: Between college dormitories and cramped apartments, young adults often live in environments that can be loud, bright or uncomfortable, making it difficult to reliably get a good night's sleep, according to Adwoa Dadzie, a doctoral candidate in biobehavioral health at Penn State.

mix_items.title: New recommendations for serrated polyposis syndrome
mix_items.summary: New consensus recommendations by the U.S. Multi-Society Task Force (MSTF) on Colorectal Cancer (CRC) address serrated polyposis syndrome (SPS), which is the most common gastrointestinal polyp syndrome yet is widely underrecognized and often goes undiagnosed. SPS is a clinical syndrome characterized by an increased number of serrated lesions and is associated with an increased risk of CRC.

mix_items.title: SpaceX launches 4 astronauts on a fast track to the International Space Station
mix_items.summary: Four astronauts rocketed into orbit Thursday on a space station mission that will stretch until spring, among them a Canadian whose wife will give birth while he's away.

mix_items.title: Largest-ever jaguar analysis identifies how populations are connected across the Americas
mix_items.summary: An international team of researchers has produced the most comprehensive assessment to date of connectivity across the jaguar's range, identifying key habitats and movement corridors that could help guide conservation efforts for the Americas' largest cat.

mix_items.title: Celebrity accounts reveal distinctive victim-blaming in deepfake sexual abuse
mix_items.summary: Celebrity victim-survivors of deepfake sexual abuse face distinctive forms of victim-blaming, harassment and barriers to justice, according to new research led by Irish researchers.

mix_items.title: Urban environments may be the ultimate training grounds for invasive species
mix_items.summary: As cities grow and urban sprawl expands, could these changing landscapes be giving invasive species a competitive edge? Scientists at the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS) say the answer may be yes, according to a new study from the UF/IFAS Invasion Science Institute.

mix_items.title: Hazelwood redevelopment suggests neighborhood investment can advance without typical displacement pressures
mix_items.summary: Neighborhood investments meant to improve housing and opportunity often spark fears of gentrification and displacement. That worry is playing out in Pittsburgh's Hazelwood neighborhood, where a stalled Second Avenue housing project sits blocks from the 178-acre (72-hectare) Hazelwood Green riverfront development.

mix_items.title: Sex-like DNA exchange in starving bacteria occurs over 100 times more often than spontaneous mutations
mix_items.summary: How do bacteria adapt when resources run low? ISTA researchers have found that, under starvation stress, E. coli can use bacteriophages and CRISPR-Cas immunity to transfer and incorporate DNA, accelerating genetic reshuffling. The process resembles a primitive form of sexual reproduction and may help bacterial populations adapt to changing conditions. The findings were published in Molecular Biology and Evolution.

mix_items.title: Does a deeper voice make men more attractive? These researchers have the answer
mix_items.summary: During puberty, as boys transition into men, the dramatic drop in their vocal pitch has sparked a long-running debate among scientists. Why did such deep voices evolve in the first place? Was it to attract female mates or to intimidate rival men? Or perhaps something else is going on.

mix_items.title: Novel treatment combination improves progression-free survival in most common form of metastatic breast cancer
mix_items.summary: Patients with estrogen receptor-positive (ER+), HER-2-negative advanced breast cancer experienced significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) when treated with an oral combination regimen that included giredestrant, a novel, next-generation selective ER degrader and full antagonist (SERD), compared with a standard combination approach. These findings, from the phase 3 evERA Breast Cancer study, were published today in the New England Journal of Medicine. Initial results of the evERA study were presented at the 2025 Congress of the European Society of Medical Oncology.

mix_items.title: Magnetic therapy headset shows improved cognitive function and mood in people with long COVID
mix_items.summary: A new study led by researchers from the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai and published in Brain Communications found that a transcranial low-amplitude magnetic field intervention delivered twice weekly into the brain through a noninvasive headset was associated with improvements in several measures of cognitive function and emotional well-being in people experiencing cognitive impairment associated with long COVID.

mix_items.title: Study finds hidden mutation rates may shape cancer risk
mix_items.summary: A new study by scientists at City of Hope and TGen, part of City of Hope, found surprisingly large differences in the number of mutations present in the organs of healthy individuals. Some study participants had mutation counts similar to those typically found in cancer patients. These results provide an explanation for why some individuals ultimately develop cancer, opening the door to improved approaches to cancer risk assessment and prevention.

mix_items.title: Initiative standardizes evaluation of ICU discharge readiness
mix_items.summary: A standardized process to evaluate patients for their readiness to be discharged from an intensive care unit (ICU) can help reduce readmissions while providing clarity and supporting collaboration among the interprofessional team, according to a study published in Critical Care Nurse.

mix_items.summary: Gorillas are among humans’ closest relatives, with a common ancestor dating back around 8 to 10 million years. Both species of gorilla alive today are on the edge of extinction: The eastern gorilla (Gorilla beringei) is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List, while the western gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) is critically endangered. Growing up in the village of Sindhupalchok, east of the capital, Kathmandu, she spent much of her time helping her mother around the house and in the fields while her father worked in the city. mix_items.summary: Nearly two years after U.S. President Trump’s decision to dismantle international development agency USAID removed nearly $1 billion from global conservation and environment funding, the agency’s absence is being felt across the world, new analysis says. The abrupt termination of around 5,200 contracts in early 2025 ended support for activities as varied as plastic waste […]

mix_items.summary: Here is the argument I want to make plainly, before anything else: the biodiversity credit market should stop trying to copy carbon’s trick of reducing everything to one tradable unit, and should instead measure its own success by how continuously and independently a claim can be verified. Chasing a single elegant number, the way carbon […]

mix_items.title: A major risk of breast cancer screening may have been overestimated for decades
mix_items.summary: A new analysis suggests mammograms may lead to far less breast cancer overdiagnosis than some earlier studies indicated. Researchers reexamined all eight major randomized screening trials and accounted for differences in follow-up time, screening frequency, and screening after trials ended. Their results were consistent with an overdiagnosis rate below 5%, rather than estimates approaching 30% to 50%.

mix_items.title: That fresh cleaning smell could be filling your home with nanoparticles
mix_items.summary: Researchers found that scented cleaners can react with ozone indoors to create billions or trillions of invisible nanoparticles that can penetrate deep into the lungs. The pollution forms within minutes and, in some cases, may produce an inhaled particle dose comparable to or greater than standing near heavy traffic.

mix_items.title: Zepbound and Mounjaro may turn on the body’s calorie-burning brown fat
mix_items.summary: Tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound, activated calorie-burning brown fat in obese mice, revealing a potential metabolic effect beyond appetite suppression. If confirmed in humans, the finding could help explain the drug’s powerful benefits and inspire more comprehensive treatments for obesity and diabetes.

mix_items.title: REM sleep paradox: Dreaming may drain the brain’s energy even as fuel supply rises
mix_items.summary: Scientists discovered a surprising energy paradox in the brain during REM sleep, the stage most closely associated with dreaming. Blood supply to the brain begins increasing even before REM starts, but neurons’ immediately available energy, measured as ATP, then drops. The finding suggests that dreaming may require such intense internal processing that neurons consume energy faster than it can be replenished.

mix_items.title: Don’t toss cannabis leaves: They may contain rare compounds with medical potential
mix_items.summary: Scientists discovered rare flavoalkaloids in Cannabis leaves for the first time, along with dozens of other phenolic compounds that had never been reported in the plant. The findings suggest that Cannabis leaves, often discarded as waste, may contain a surprisingly rich source of potentially useful chemicals.

mix_items.title: Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once
mix_items.summary: A new needle-thin brain implant can record neural activity, deliver drugs, and stimulate multiple brain regions using a single flexible fiber. Successful tests in mice suggest it could give scientists a more precise, less invasive way to study the brain and may eventually help treat neurological disorders such as epilepsy.

mix_items.title: Stanford scientists discover the human brain may actually be two separate organs
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found that the human brain develops from two distinct cellular systems, suggesting that evolution fused together two ancient nervous systems with very different jobs. The discovery also allowed researchers to grow human hindbrain neurons in the lab, opening new possibilities for studying ALS, spinal muscular atrophy, and other brainstem diseases.

mix_items.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
mix_items.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

mix_items.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

mix_items.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
mix_items.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

mix_items.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
mix_items.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

mix_items.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
mix_items.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

mix_items.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
mix_items.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

mix_items.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
mix_items.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.
